source: UCI Online Retail — a UK gift wholesaler, 1 Dec 2010 to 9 Dec 2011

excluded.label: Exact duplicate rows
excluded.why: Byte-identical to an earlier row — same invoice, product, quantity and timestamp.
excluded.impact: None. Keeping them would inflate revenue.

excluded.label: Cancelled invoices
excluded.why: Invoice number begins with C. These are returns, carrying negative quantities.
excluded.impact: Revenue here is GROSS of returns. Net revenue would be lower.

excluded.label: Non-positive quantity
excluded.why: Zero or negative quantity outside the cancellation flag — adjustments and write-offs.

excluded.label: Zero or negative price
excluded.why: Samples, giveaways and manual adjustments priced at or below zero.
excluded.impact: Units shipped are undercounted; these were real goods leaving the warehouse.

findings.headline: 5.7% of the catalogue earns half the revenue
findings.detail: 230 of 4,026 products account for 50% of takings. The top line alone is 1.9%.
findings.action: Protect stock on those lines first; a stockout there is not recoverable elsewhere.
findings.basis: Revenue by description across 524,878 clean rows.
findings.why: Rests on quantity x price, present on every retained row. But the ranking includes non-goods line items — postage and fees are £383,144 (3.6%) of revenue, and the top entry is a delivery charge.

findings.headline: 84.6% of revenue comes from one country
findings.detail: The United Kingdom accounts for 84.6% of takings across 38 countries served.
findings.action: Growth has to come from abroad, or from basket size at home. There is no third lever.
findings.basis: Revenue grouped by the Country field.
findings.why: Country is present on every row and needs no inference.

findings.headline: Repeat customers drive 93.1% of identified revenue
findings.detail: 65.6% of identifiable customers ordered more than once, and they produce 93.1% of the revenue we can attribute.
findings.action: Retention is worth more than acquisition here. Start with the second order.
findings.basis: Customers with a recorded ID only — 74.8% of rows.
findings.why: 132,186 rows (25.2%) have no customer ID. If anonymous sales skew one-off, this OVERSTATES repeat share.

findings.headline: November 2011 earned 2.9x what February 2011 did
findings.detail: Peak November 2011 at £1,503,867 against February 2011 at £522,546. The pattern is a hard autumn run-up into Christmas.
findings.action: Working capital should be timed to the run-up, not spread evenly across the year.
findings.basis: Monthly revenue, excluding the truncated final month.
findings.why: One full year only, so seasonality cannot be separated from a one-off good year.

limits: One year of data. Seasonality and growth cannot be told apart from a single cycle.
132,186 rows (25.2%) have no customer ID, so every per-customer figure describes the identifiable subset, not the business.
Revenue is GROSS. 9,251 cancelled invoices were removed rather than netted off.
The final month stops on 2011-12-09. Its apparent fall is the calendar, not demand.

The product ranking mixes goods with charges. Postage, bank fees and manual adjustments are booked as line items and account for £383,144 (3.6% of revenue) — the top entry, “Dotcom Postage”, is a delivery fee, not a product.
